strengths: PST addresses a relevant problem in multimodal NLP: gender stereotypes in images containing multiple people. Extending evaluation from occupational identities to organizational power adds a useful perspective.

The occupational experiment systematically covers 800 prompts, including both orders of each occupation pair. Tables 2 and 11 provide substantial descriptive evidence of conventional stereotype adherence under paired prompting, particularly the increase in male-stereotyped occupation SS from −30.00 to 49.74.

Using three human annotators and reporting Fleiss’ kappa values of 0.88–0.92 supports annotation consistency. The comparison with BLIP usefully demonstrates why an unchecked automated evaluator would be unreliable in this setting.
The appendix provides occupation lists, prompt templates, annotation instructions, and detailed results. These make the basic evaluation procedure understandable and support further investigation.
weaknesses: The principal obstacle to a clear Findings recommendation is the interpretation of SS. It measures signed stereotype adherence, whereas Section 3.1 defines fairness through equal gender probabilities. Opposing deviations can cancel: Table 2 averages female SS of 50 and male SS of −30 into an apparently low overall score of 10. Thus, the results establish increased conventional-stereotype adherence more directly than increased overall gender bias or an initially fair baseline. Direction and magnitude of imbalance should be evaluated separately.

The single-person baseline contains only three images per identity, making occupation-level estimates particularly unstable. No confidence intervals or statistical tests accompany the amplification claims. Additional sampling and uncertainty estimates accounting for dependence within images and repeated occupations are needed, especially for the smaller organizational-power difference of 14.36 SS points.

The evaluation assumes that requested identities appear at their specified positions, but does not report a systematic DALL-E-3 audit of role correctness, position swaps, or extra/missing people. Agreement about gender presentation does not validate occupation or power-role assignment. Although annotators can select 'Cannot Identify,' its frequency and treatment in aggregation are unspecified.

The headline percentage of 'biased images' needs an explicit reference distribution. Under independent, gender-balanced generation, a two-person image has a 75% chance of containing at least one stereotype-consistent individual. Consequently, Figure 4’s 74.3% PST(Any) rate alone is not evidence of bias. The much higher-than-chance PST(Both) rate is informative and should be distinguished from this misleading headline interpretation.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the useful appendix. The paper omits generation dates, precise access/configuration details, and the actual sampled organizational-role prompts; automatic prompt rewriting, if used, also needs documentation. Code and data are only promised upon acceptance. Section 3.2.2 additionally reports 944 prompts, conflicting with the stated total of 1,952, and should clearly distinguish constructed prompts from evaluated samples.

The mitigation conclusions exceed the experiment. One intervention, with occupational testing restricted to the five most biased occupations per gender, cannot establish a general failure of prompt-based mitigation. The organizational-power change from 18.98 to −11.12 crosses zero but also reduces its absolute magnitude; without uncertainty estimates, systematic reverse bias is unestablished. Broader conclusions should also be bounded to the single evaluated model and limited prompt formulations.
